verses.text: Now Sarai, Abram’s wife, bore him no children. She had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Hagar.
Sarai said to Abram, “See now, Yahweh has restrained me from bearing. Please go in to my servant. It may be that I will obtain children by her.” Abram listened to the voice of Sarai.
Sarai, Abram’s wife, took Hagar the Egyptian, her servant, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to Abram her husband to be his wife.
He went in to Hagar, and she conceived. When she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was despised in her eyes.
Sarai said to Abram, “This wrong is your fault. I gave my servant into your bosom, and when she saw that she had conceived, I was despised in her eyes. Yahweh judge between me and you.”
But Abram said to Sarai, “Behold, your maid is in your hand. Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.” Sarai dealt harshly with her, and she fled from her face.
Yahweh’s angel found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness, by the fountain on the way to Shur.
He said, “Hagar, Sarai’s servant, where did you come from? Where are you going?” She said, “I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Return to your mistress, and submit yourself under her hands.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “I will greatly multiply your offspring,  that they will not be counted for multitude.”
Yahweh’s angel said to her, “Behold, you are with child, and will bear a son. You shall call his name Ishmael, because Yahweh has heard your affliction.
He will be like a wild donkey among men. His hand will be against every man, and every man’s hand against him. He will live opposite all of his brothers.”
She called the name of Yahweh who spoke to her, “You are a God who sees,” for she said, “Have I even stayed alive after seeing him?”
Therefore the well was called Beer Lahai Roi.  Behold, it is between Kadesh and Bered.
Hagar bore a son for Abram. Abram called the name of his son, whom Hagar bore, Ishmael.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abram.

footnotes.content: Sarai's barrenness weighs heavy after ten years in Canaan. I have learned that God's promises can feel long delayed, yet the Lord who called Abram remains faithful even when His timing doesn't match our hopes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It grieves me to see a godly couple taking matters into their own hands. Sarai offers a human solution, Abram listens to her voice instead of waiting on Yahweh's word — and how often I too try to help God accomplish what He has already promised to do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After a decade of waiting, impatience bears fruit in a hasty act. Sarai gives Hagar to Abram as wife, a custom of the age but not the path of faith. I am reminded that even believers can choose expediency over trust in the God who keeps His promises.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sin rarely stays contained to the one who initiated it. Hagar conceives and looks with contempt on Sarai; what was meant as a 'solution' has already begun to produce strife. Our grasping for blessing often turns the gift into a source of bitterness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sarai blames Abram for the very wrong she had proposed. It is a painful thing when the fruit of our own scheme is turned against us. How merciful that our great Judge, Yahweh, is the One who ultimately rights every wrong — and our hope rests in Him, not in human vengeance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram abdicates his responsibility to his servant and wife, saying 'do to her whatever is good in your eyes.' A man of faith here shows cowardly passivity. I pray the Lord Jesus, our true and faithful Husband and Protector, would rule our homes with strength and tenderness where we have failed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is mercy: Yahweh's angel finds Hagar by the fountain in the wilderness on the way to Shur. This is no mere messenger — in Genesis the 'angel of Yahweh' often speaks as Yahweh Himself. The God who made promises to Abram now pursues an Egyptian servant girl whom everyone else has discarded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The God who sees asks Hagar two gentle questions: 'Where did you come from? Where are you going?' He already knows the answers, but He draws her out to speak. Our Lord still condescends to ask us about our sorrow, that we might bring it to Him who cares.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The command is hard: return and submit. Yet it comes from the One who has just sought her out and will soon bless her. Sometimes the path of repentance and faith is not to run from difficult duty, but to return under the covering of One who has promised to be near to the afflicted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh Himself makes a personal promise to Hagar: He will greatly multiply her offspring. This is free grace to one with no claim on Abram's covenant. The God of the covenant stoops to bless the overlooked, a foretaste of how He delights to show mercy to the lowly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel tells Hagar to call her son Ishmael, 'because Yahweh has heard your affliction.' The name is itself an anchor of hope: El Shama, God hears. Long before we call, the God who sees (v.13) is also the God who hears the cry of the wounded and cast down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A sobering prophecy about Ishmael — a man of conflict, living at odds. Yet even this is spoken by the merciful One who has just met Hagar in her affliction. God's justice and mercy often travel together; He tells the truth, but He tells it to one He has already determined to bless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hagar gives Yahweh a name: 'El Roi' — 'You are a God who sees.' She has seen the God who sees her. No one else in that moment had looked after her with care, but the Living God had sought her out in the desert. What comfort for all who feel forgotten: our Savior has set His eyes upon us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call the well Beer Lahai Roi, 'the Well of the Living One who sees me.' Between Kadesh and Bered, a desert spring becomes a monument of grace. For those who belong to Jesus, every place of mercy where the Lord met us becomes an altar of remembrance: He is the Living One who still sees and saves His own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hagar bears a son to Abram as promised, and Abram names him Ishmael in obedience to the word from Yahweh. Both the servant girl and the aged patriarch do as they are told in this moment. I am grateful that the God of all grace uses even broken obedience to bring about what He has spoken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abram is eighty-six years old when Ishmael is born — a long life, yet still marked by waiting and by failure. It reminds me that age and faithfulness don't always grow together. But our hope is not in the strength of Abram's faith, but in the faithfulness of the God who would one day send a true Son to keep all His promises.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
